USER REQUEST:
Write a polynomial-time reduction from SAT to Independent Set. problems.py defines both problems: SOURCE is SAT and TARGET is Independent Set. The SOURCE and TARGET class docstrings give the exact instance formats, yes-conditions and edge cases.

PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = Sat
SAT (CNF satisfiability).

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[literal, ...], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m. A literal is +v (v is true) or -v (v is false).
  * A clause is a list of any number of literals, including none.
    Literals may repeat, and a clause may contain both v and -v.
  * Literal order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes every
clause contain at least one true literal.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is satisfiable (yes). An empty
clause [] can never be satisfied, so any formula containing one is no.

TARGET = IndependentSet
Independent Set.

Instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...], "k": k}
  * Vertices are 0..n-1. Edges are undirected pairs [u, v] with u != v;
    [u, v] and [v, u] are the same edge and may not both appear.
  * k is any integer.

Yes iff the graph has an independent set of AT LEAST k vertices: k
vertices with no edge between any two of them.

Edge cases: k <= 0 is always yes. k > n is always no. With no edges,
every set of vertices is independent.

WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-dcr6we7h

    reduce(instance) -> instance

The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

"""Polynomial-time reduction from SAT to Independent Set.

Construction (the standard one):
  * For every occurrence of a literal in a clause, create one vertex.
    Vertex ids are assigned in order of clause, then literal position.
  * Inside each clause, add an edge between every pair of its vertices,
    so an independent set can pick at most one literal per clause.
  * Between clauses, add an edge between every pair of contradictory
    literals (v and -v), so a consistent assignment is forced.
  * Set k = number of clauses.

A satisfying assignment picks one true literal per clause: these choices
are pairwise non-adjacent (one per clause, no contradictions), giving an
independent set of size = #clauses. Conversely, any independent set of
size k = #clauses must contain exactly one vertex per clause, and since
no contradictory pair is chosen, setting those literals true (and the
other variables arbitrarily) satisfies every clause.

Edge cases:
  * No clauses -> k = 0, empty graph -> yes (k <= 0).
  * Empty clause -> it contributes no vertex, so the maximum independent
    set is at most (#nonempty clauses) < k -> no.
"""


def reduce(instance):
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]
    clauses = instance["clauses"]

    n = 0
    # vertices[i] = list of vertex ids for clause i
    vertices = []
    for clause in clauses:
        ids = []
        for _literal in clause:
            ids.append(n)
            n += 1
        vertices.append(ids)

    edges = set()

    def add_edge(u, v):
        if u == v:
            return
        a, b = (u, v) if u < v else (v, u)
        edges.add((a, b))

    # Edges among literals of the same clause.
    for ids in vertices:
        for i in range(len(ids)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(ids)):
                add_edge(ids[i], ids[j])

    # Edges between contradictory literals in different clauses.
    # Map literal value -> list of vertex ids carrying that literal.
    occurrences = {}
    for clause, ids in zip(clauses, vertices):
        for literal, vid in zip(clause, ids):
            occurrences.setdefault(literal, []).append(vid)

    for literal, vids in occurrences.items():
        opposite = occurrences.get(-literal)
        if not opposite:
            continue
        for u in vids:
            for v in opposite:
                add_edge(u, v)

    edge_list = [[u, v] for (u, v) in sorted(edges)]

    return {"n": n, "edges": edge_list, "k": len(clauses)}
EOF
